description: Hi everyone! I’m a high school student and tech enthusiast passionate about combining software development, robotics, and applied math to tackle ambitious projects. I have hands-on experience in full-stack coding (Java, Python, web development), edge hardware/embedded systems, and local developer setup (Git, Docker, APIs). Additionally, I actively work with robotics platforms and computer vision hardware.
summary:
The project is a public website that turns SPHEREx sky images into a 3D "time cube", so anyone can spot things that move or change. It answers the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge: enter sky coordinates, see how that patch changes over time.
• The cube. Frames of one sky patch are stacked with time as the vertical axis. A fixed star becomes a vertical line. A moving object becomes a slanted line.
• The search. Tilting the cube is the search tool. Look along a slanted line and that object snaps into focus while the stars smear.
• The second axis. Flip the vertical axis from time to wavelength and the same cube shows SPHEREx's 102 infrared colours.
• The inspiration. Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by blinking two photographic plates. This blinks 16 years of sky in every direction at once.
details:
SPHEREx Time Cube is a free website that lets anyone see how a patch of sky changes over time. Type in a target name or coordinates and we pull every SPHEREx image of that spot from NASA’s archive. The images are lined up and stacked into a 3D cube, with time going up the side. A star that stays put shows up as a straight vertical line. Anything that moves shows up as a slanted one.

To search, you tilt the cube. Line it up with a slanted line and the moving object snaps into a sharp point while the background stars blur out. Under the hood this is shift-and-stack, a standard technique for finding faint movers. A motion map tries many possible motions at once and points you to the best ones.

You can also flip the cube so it stacks by wavelength instead of time, which shows SPHEREx’s 102 infrared colours. Click any pixel to see its spectrum, or track its brightness over time for variable stars. Other features:

WISE images back to 2010 stretch the timeline to 16 years
Gaia star overlays
Side-by-side comparison of two dates
A practice mode with a fake moving object
Shareable links that save your exact view

When SPHEREx releases new data, the tool fetches just the new images and updates its cubes.

Why it matters

SPHEREx will image over a billion objects, far too many for scientists to check alone. Most known brown dwarfs and comets were found by volunteers comparing sky images, and we wanted to make that easy for students and citizen scientists. Everything runs in the browser, with no login and only public NASA data. We tested it on all five challenge targets. It recovers the known motion of WISE 0855, a fast-moving brown dwarf.

How we built it

Frontend: TypeScript, Vite and Three.js
Backend: Python and FastAPI
Astronomy: Astropy, PyVO, reproject, NumPy and SciPy
Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA, Gaia DR3, unWISE and SIMBAD
Deployment and testing: Docker on Render, with pytest
No hardware needed

What makes it creative

Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by flipping back and forth between two photos of the sky. Our tool does the same thing with 16 years of sky, in every direction at once. Searching becomes something you do with your hands: tilt the cube until something comes into focus.

What we thought about

Honesty came first. Anything the tool highlights is labelled a “candidate,” never a discovery. It also warns you when a variable star might be faking motion or when a bright star is saturated. We also thought about accuracy, beginners (a guided tour, a glossary and practice mode) and speed (you pick the field of view, and results are cached). The code is open source and every result can be reproduced from public data.
